question: What must a give-way vessel do under Rule 16 of the Inland Navigation Rules, distinct from the stand-on vessel's duty to hold course and speed?
choice_a: So far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel
choice_b: Wait until the last possible moment so the stand-on vessel can see the maneuver clearly
choice_c: Hold its exact course and speed just like the stand-on vessel
choice_d: Make only very small, gradual course changes so as not to alarm the other operator
explanation: Rule 16 requires a give-way vessel to take early and substantial action, so far as possible, to keep well clear of the other vessel -- the opposite of waiting or making only small, ambiguous adjustments.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 16 (action by give-way vessel), 33 CFR 83.16

question: Under the Rule 18 responsibility hierarchy, which vessels must a power-driven vessel underway generally keep out of the way of?
choice_a: Only other power-driven vessels of the same size
choice_b: A vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel
choice_c: No other vessel, since power-driven vessels always have the right of way
choice_d: Only vessels flying a distress flag
explanation: Rule 18 sets a hierarchy of responsibility: a power-driven vessel underway must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in fishing, and a sailing vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (responsibilities between vessels), 33 CFR 83.18

question: Even though a sailing vessel is generally privileged over a power-driven vessel, which vessels must a sailing vessel itself still keep out of the way of under Rule 18?
choice_a: No vessel; a sailing vessel outranks every other vessel in every situation
choice_c: A vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing
explanation: The right-of-way hierarchy is not simply 'sail beats power' -- a sailing vessel must still keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (responsibilities between vessels), 33 CFR 83.18

question: For right-of-way purposes, does a recreational boat trolling a fishing line count as a 'vessel engaged in fishing' with special right-of-way status under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Yes, any boat with any fishing line in the water automatically outranks all other vessels
choice_b: Yes, but only if the boat is anchored
choice_c: The Rules do not address recreational fishing at all
choice_d: No -- the Rules specifically exclude trolling lines and other gear that does not restrict maneuverability from the 'engaged in fishing' definition, so a trolling boat is treated as an ordinary vessel
explanation: Rule 3 defines 'vessel engaged in fishing' as one using nets, lines, trawls, or gear that restricts maneuverability -- it expressly does not include trolling lines or other gear that does not restrict maneuverability, so a boat simply trolling has no special right-of-way status.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 3 (general definitions), 33 CFR 83.03

question: Precisely how do the Navigation Rules define when one vessel is 'overtaking' another?
choice_a: When approaching from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other vessel's beam -- a position from which, at night, only that vessel's sternlight (not its sidelights) would be visible
choice_b: Whenever one vessel is simply going faster than another, regardless of direction
choice_c: Only when the two vessels are on a direct head-on course
choice_d: Only when both vessels are power-driven
explanation: Rule 13 defines overtaking by angle: a vessel coming up on another from more than 22.5 degrees abaft that vessel's beam is overtaking -- the position from which, at night, only the sternlight would be seen, not either sidelight.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 13(b) (overtaking, definition), 33 CFR 83.13

question: When two sailing vessels under sail alone are approaching each other on different tacks (wind on different sides), which one must keep out of the way of the other?
choice_a: The vessel that has the wind on her starboard side
choice_b: The vessel that has the wind on her port side
choice_c: Whichever vessel is closer to shore
choice_d: Whichever vessel has the larger sail area
explanation: Rule 12 provides that when two sailing vessels are on different tacks, the vessel with the wind on her port side (port tack) must keep out of the way of the other -- the classic 'port tack gives way' rule of sailing.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 12(a)(i) (sailing vessels), 33 CFR 83.12

question: When two sailing vessels under sail alone have the wind on the same side (same tack), which vessel must keep out of the way of the other?
choice_a: The vessel to leeward must always give way to the vessel to windward
choice_b: Neither vessel has any obligation in this situation
choice_c: The vessel that is to windward must keep out of the way of the vessel that is to leeward
choice_d: The faster of the two vessels must give way
explanation: Rule 12 provides that when both sailing vessels have the wind on the same side, the vessel to windward (the side the wind is blowing from, opposite the mainsail) must keep out of the way of the vessel to leeward.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 12(a)(ii) (sailing vessels), 33 CFR 83.12

question: What does Rule 8 say about the size of a course or speed change made to avoid collision?
choice_a: It should always be as small as possible so the other operator barely notices
choice_b: Course changes are irrelevant as long as speed is reduced
choice_c: Only speed may be changed; course must never be altered to avoid collision
choice_d: It should be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar; a succession of small alterations should be avoided
explanation: Rule 8(b) requires that any alteration of course and/or speed to avoid collision be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel, whether observed visually or by radar, and warns against a series of small, ambiguous alterations.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 8(b) (action to avoid collision), 33 CFR 83.08

question: If altering course alone will not sufficiently avoid a collision, what does Rule 8 say a vessel must do?
choice_a: Slacken her speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing her means of propulsion if necessary
choice_b: Continue at the same speed regardless, since only course changes are permitted under the Rules
choice_c: Increase speed to clear the area before the other vessel arrives
choice_d: Sound the horn continuously instead of maneuvering
explanation: Rule 8(e) requires that if necessary to avoid collision or to allow more time to assess the situation, a vessel must slacken her speed, or take all way off by stopping or reversing her means of propulsion.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 8(e) (action to avoid collision), 33 CFR 83.08

question: In a narrow channel, what obligation does Rule 9 place on a vessel less than 20 meters in length or a sailing vessel with respect to a larger vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel?
choice_a: It has no special obligation and may cross the channel at any time
choice_b: It must not impede the passage of the vessel that can navigate safely only within the channel
choice_c: It must always anchor and let the larger vessel pass first
choice_d: Only sailing vessels have this obligation, not smaller power-driven vessels
explanation: Rule 9(b) provides that a vessel of less than 20 meters in length, or a sailing vessel, must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway, since the larger vessel has no room to maneuver outside it.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9(b) (narrow channels), 33 CFR 83.09

question: Under Rule 9, what must a vessel crossing a narrow channel do with respect to vessels that can navigate only within that channel?
choice_a: It has an absolute right to cross at any point regardless of other traffic
choice_b: It must sound five short blasts before every crossing, regardless of traffic
choice_c: It must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within the narrow channel or fairway
choice_d: Crossing a narrow channel is prohibited entirely
explanation: Rule 9(d) requires a vessel crossing a narrow channel or fairway to avoid impeding the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel, since that vessel cannot leave the channel to avoid a crossing boat.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9(d) (narrow channels), 33 CFR 83.09

question: In a meeting or crossing situation between power-driven vessels in sight of one another, what does two short blasts of the horn mean under Rule 34?
choice_b: I am overtaking you on your port side
choice_c: I do not understand your intentions
choice_d: I intend to leave you on my starboard side (I am altering my course to port)
explanation: Under Rule 34(a), two short blasts in a meeting or crossing situation means 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side,' indicating the signaling vessel is altering course to port -- the counterpart to one short blast for altering to starboard.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34(a) (maneuvering and warning signals), 33 CFR 83.34

question: When one power-driven vessel intends to overtake another power-driven vessel, Rule 34(c) gives the overtaking vessel its own separate whistle signals. What does one short blast mean in this specific overtaking context?
choice_a: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side
choice_b: I intend to overtake you on your port side
choice_c: I am altering course to starboard in a head-on meeting
choice_d: I am anchoring immediately ahead of you
explanation: Rule 34(c) gives overtaking situations their own signal meanings distinct from ordinary meeting/crossing signals: one short blast means 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side,' and two short blasts means the same for the port side; the vessel being overtaken, if in agreement, sounds the same signal back.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34(c) (maneuvering and warning signals, overtaking), 33 CFR 83.34

question: What sound signal must a vessel give when nearing a bend in a channel or fairway where an obstruction may hide an approaching vessel from view?
choice_a: No signal is required if the vessel is traveling slowly
choice_b: One prolonged blast, which any approaching vessel within hearing around the bend or obstruction must answer with a prolonged blast of its own
choice_c: Five short, rapid blasts, the same as the danger signal
explanation: Rule 34(e) requires a vessel nearing a bend or an obstructed area of a channel to sound one prolonged blast, which must be answered with a prolonged blast by any approaching vessel within hearing on the other side, alerting both to each other's presence before they can see one another.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34(e) (bend signal), 33 CFR 83.34

question: According to the Navigation Rules' own definitions, roughly how long is a 'short blast' compared to a 'prolonged blast'?
choice_a: A short blast is 10 seconds; a prolonged blast is 30 seconds
choice_b: Both terms refer to the exact same duration
choice_c: A short blast is about 1 second; a prolonged blast is 4 to 6 seconds
choice_d: A short blast is 4 to 6 seconds; a prolonged blast is about 1 second
explanation: Rule 32 defines a 'short blast' as a blast of about 1 second's duration and a 'prolonged blast' as a blast of from 4 to 6 seconds' duration -- the timing itself is part of what distinguishes the different maneuvering and warning signals.

question: Under Rule 19, if a vessel detects another vessel by radar alone in restricted visibility and determines a close-quarters situation is developing, which course alterations should generally be avoided (other than when overtaking)?
choice_a: There are no restrictions on which way to alter course when using radar
choice_b: Altering course to starboard is always prohibited in restricted visibility
choice_c: Any course alteration at all is prohibited until the other vessel is visually sighted
choice_d: Altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, and altering course toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam
explanation: Rule 19(d) advises against altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam (other than one being overtaken) and against altering course toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam, since these radar-based maneuvers are more likely to create rather than resolve a close-quarters situation.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 19(d) (conduct of vessels in restricted visibility), 33 CFR 83.19

question: What does Rule 19 require of a power-driven vessel's engines while navigating in or near restricted visibility, in addition to proceeding at a safe speed?
choice_a: The engines shall be ready for immediate maneuver
choice_b: The engines must be shut off entirely until visibility improves
choice_c: There is no engine-related requirement beyond ordinary operation
choice_d: The engines must be run at maximum RPM at all times
explanation: Rule 19(b) requires a power-driven vessel to have her engines ready for immediate maneuver while proceeding at a safe speed adapted to restricted visibility conditions, so she can react quickly if another vessel is detected.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 19(b) (conduct of vessels in restricted visibility), 33 CFR 83.19

question: What special obligation does Rule 18 place on a seaplane on the water in relation to other vessels?
choice_a: A seaplane always has the right of way over every other vessel
choice_b: A seaplane must keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation
choice_c: Seaplanes are entirely exempt from the Navigation Rules
choice_d: A seaplane only needs to give way to other seaplanes
explanation: Rule 18 provides that, in normal circumstances, a seaplane on the water must keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation, reflecting its limited maneuverability and visibility relative to other traffic.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (responsibilities between vessels), 33 CFR 83.18
